tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 1. Looking Up. In 1851 the French physicist Léon Foucault hung a 28-kilogram metal ball on a wire 67 meters long from the dome of the Panthéon, a huge stone building in Paris, and set it swinging. A swinging weight like this, a pendulum, keeps swinging back and forth along the same line unless something pushes it sideways. Nothing pushed Foucault’s pendulum. Yet as visitors watched, the line of its swing crept slowly around the floor, about 11 degrees every hour. The pendulum was holding its line. The floor, the building, the city and all the ground under Paris were turning beneath it. You are turning right now, too. That turning, together with two other motions of Earth and the Moon, explains most of what you will see the first time you really look up. This chapter starts where every astronomer starts: outside, looking up, with nothing but your eyes. Section 1.1 explains why the Sun, Moon and stars rise and set, and how Foucault showed that it is the ground, not the sky, that turns. Section 1.2 explains why the Moon changes shape over a month. Section 1.3 explains summer and winter and clears away the most common wrong explanation. Along the way you meet the two tools used in every later chapter: the pocket scale model, in which the Sun is a ball about 20 cm (8 inches) across and Earth is a peppercorn, and your sky diary, which you start at the end of this chapter. In Chapter 2 the scale model grows outward to hold all the planets.

tracks.label: 1.1 Day, night and the spinning Earth
tracks.text: Section 1 point 1. Day, night and the spinning Earth. Watch the sky for a day and a night and you will see a pattern. The Sun comes up in the east, climbs across the sky and goes down in the west. After dark the stars do the same, and so does the Moon. For thousands of years most people assumed that the sky was turning around a motionless Earth. In fact Earth spins like a top around an axis, an imaginary line through the North Pole, the center of the planet and the South Pole. One full turn is called a rotation. Measured against the distant stars, one rotation takes 23 hours 56 minutes, a sidereal day. Measured from one noon to the next, the day we set our clocks by, it takes 24 hours, a solar day. The extra four minutes come from Earth’s yearly trip around the Sun, which you will meet in Section 1.3. At any moment the Sun lights one half of Earth. On that half it is day, and on the other half it is night. Earth turns from west to east, so each morning it carries you out of the dark half and into the light. That moment is sunrise. In the evening it carries you back into the dark half, and that is sunset (Figure 1.1). Because the ground under you is moving toward the east, everything in the sky seems to slide the other way, toward the west, the way trees seem to slide backward past the window of a moving train. Earth turns fast. A point on the equator travels about 1,670 km (1,040 miles) every hour, faster than a jet airliner flies. You do not feel it because the motion is smooth and steady, just as you cannot feel a smooth flight with your eyes closed. Earth turns a full circle, 360 degrees, in about 24 hours, so the sky seems to turn 15 degrees every hour. You can measure angles on the sky with your own hand: held out at arm’s length, your closed fist covers about 10 degrees. Not everything in the sky moves the same amount. Earth’s axis points at a spot in the northern sky called the north celestial pole, and the stars seem to wheel around that spot once a day. A star of medium brightness, Polaris, the North Star, sits less than one degree from it, so Polaris hardly moves while all the other stars circle it. From the Southern Hemisphere, Polaris is below the horizon, and no bright star marks the south pole of the sky. For most of history nobody could tell by looking whether the sky or the ground was turning. Foucault’s pendulum settled the question. Nothing in a pendulum makes its swing turn by itself. If Earth stood still, the swing would stay lined up with the same marks on the floor all day. Instead, at the latitude of Paris, the line of the swing turns about 11 degrees an hour and goes all the way around in about 32 hours. That is what a spinning Earth predicts. At the North Pole the floor would turn a full circle under the pendulum in one rotation. At the equator it would not turn at all, and in between the rate depends on latitude. Foucault’s report was read to the French Academy of Sciences in February 1851, and within months copies of his pendulum were swinging in cities around the world. To keep sizes and distances straight, this book uses one scale model all the way through, based on Guy Ottewell’s Thousand-Yard Model. In it, every 100,000 miles (about 160,000 km) of real space shrinks to one inch (2.5 cm). The Sun becomes a ball about 20 cm (8 inches) across, the size of a bowling ball. Earth becomes a peppercorn about 2 mm wide, sitting about 24 m (26 yards) from the ball, roughly the length of two school buses. Picture that peppercorn spinning once a day while the bowling ball lights the half facing it. Every sunrise anyone has ever seen happened on that turning speck. Keep the peppercorn in mind. In the next section we add the Moon beside it, and in Chapter 2 we walk out to the other planets. A common misconception: The Sun moves across the sky from east to west, so it must be going around us every day. In fact, The Sun’s daily trip across the sky is caused by Earth turning from west to east once a day, which carries us past the Sun the way a train carries you past a tree. Foucault’s pendulum shows that the ground itself is turning. Earth does travel around the Sun, but that takes a year, not a day (Section 1.3).

tracks.label: 1.2 The Moon and its phases
tracks.text: Section 1 point 2. The Moon and its phases. The Moon is the nearest world to us and the easiest to watch. It is a ball of rock about 3,475 km across, a little more than a quarter as wide as Earth, and it circles Earth at an average distance of about 384,400 km. Light crosses that gap in about 1.3 seconds. The Moon makes no light of its own; its glow is sunlight bouncing off its gray, dusty surface. Add it to the pocket scale model and it becomes a speck about half a millimeter wide, like a grain of sand, circling the peppercorn Earth only about 6 cm (2.4 inches) away. The bowling-ball Sun is still 24 m off. So at any moment, sunlight reaches the Moon and Earth from almost exactly the same direction. The Sun always lights half of the Moon, the half that faces the Sun. What changes over a month is how much of that lit half is turned toward us. The Moon travels around Earth along a path called an orbit, and the shape of the lit part we see from Earth is called the Moon’s phase. When the Moon is roughly between Earth and the Sun, its lit half faces away from us and we see nothing: this is the new Moon. Then a thin sliver of the lit half comes into view, a crescent. About a week after new Moon we see half of the Moon’s face lit. This is a first quarter Moon, because the Moon is a quarter of the way around its orbit. Next comes a gibbous Moon, more than half lit, and about two weeks after new Moon, with the Moon on the far side of Earth from the Sun, we see the whole lit half: a full Moon (Figure 1.2). After full Moon the same shapes return in reverse order: waning gibbous, third quarter (also called last quarter), waning crescent, and new Moon again. Waxing means growing and waning means shrinking. One full cycle of phases, from new Moon to the next new Moon, takes about 29.5 days, the lunar month. Measured against the stars, the Moon actually goes once around Earth in about 27.3 days. It needs about two days more to get back to new Moon because Earth has moved along its own path around the Sun in the meantime, so the Moon must travel a little farther to line up with the Sun again. The phase also tells you when to look. Each day the Moon moves about 12 degrees farther east of the Sun, so it rises later each day, on average about 50 minutes later, though the exact delay varies. A full Moon sits opposite the Sun, so it rises around sunset, sets around sunrise and is up all night. A first quarter Moon is highest in the sky around sunset and sets around midnight. A third quarter Moon rises around midnight and is still up through the morning. A young waxing crescent hangs low in the west just after sunset. So for much of the month you can find the Moon in the daytime sky. From the Northern Hemisphere a waxing Moon is lit on its right side. From Australia or Argentina the view is flipped, and a waxing Moon is lit on its left. A daytime Moon shows that Earth’s shadow is not the cause of the phases. On a clear afternoon about a week after new Moon, you can see a half-lit Moon and the Sun in the sky at the same time, and the Moon’s lit side always points toward the Sun. Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun, so it cannot be falling on a Moon that sits off to one side of the Sun. Earth’s shadow does sometimes reach the Moon, but only at full Moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up. That event is a lunar eclipse. It does not happen every month because the Moon’s orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees, so the full Moon usually passes just above or below the shadow. One more pattern: the Moon spins once for each trip around Earth, so the same face always points toward us. The far side is not dark; it is in full sunlight at new Moon. A common misconception: The Moon changes shape because Earth’s shadow covers part of it. In fact, Phases come from seeing more or less of the Moon’s sunlit half as it goes around Earth. Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun, so it can only reach a full Moon, and then only during a lunar eclipse. A crescent Moon is seen close to the Sun in the sky, where Earth’s shadow could never fall on it.

tracks.label: 1.3 Seasons
tracks.text: Section 1 point 3. Seasons. Ask people why summer is warm and many will say that Earth is closer to the Sun then. It sounds sensible, because a campfire feels hotter when you step closer. The numbers say otherwise. Earth’s path around the Sun is very nearly a circle. Its distance ranges from about 147.1 million km at the closest point, called perihelion, to about 152.1 million km at the farthest, called aphelion, a difference of only about 3 percent. And Earth reaches perihelion in early January, in the middle of the northern winter. In the pocket scale model the peppercorn sits about 24 m from the bowling ball, and over a whole year that distance changes by less than one meter, about one long step. A second clue settles it. Seasons are opposite in the two halves of the planet. In December, while people in Canada shovel snow, people in Australia and Argentina go to the beach. If distance caused the seasons, the whole Earth would have summer at the same time. The real cause is a tilt. Earth’s axis is not straight up and down compared with its path around the Sun; it leans by about 23.4 degrees, Earth’s axial tilt. The axis also keeps pointing the same way in space all year, toward Polaris. So around June 21 the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and around December 21 it leans away (Figure 1.3). These two dates are the solstices. Halfway between, around March 20 and September 22, neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun. These are the equinoxes, when day and night are close to 12 hours each almost everywhere on Earth. Leaning toward the Sun matters in two ways. First, the Sun climbs higher in the sky, and sunlight from high up is more concentrated. Shine a flashlight straight down at a table and you get a small, bright circle. Tilt the flashlight and the same light spreads into a bigger, dimmer oval. Low winter sunlight is like the tilted flashlight: the same sunshine is spread over more ground, so each square meter gets less. Second, the days are longer, and more hours of sunshine with fewer hours of night means more heating. At 40 degrees north, the latitude of Philadelphia, Madrid and Beijing, the noon Sun stands about 73 degrees above the horizon at the June solstice but only about 27 degrees at the December solstice. The day lasts roughly 15 hours in June and roughly 9 hours in December. The same tilt explains the most extreme places on Earth. At and north of the Arctic Circle, about 66.6 degrees north, the Sun stays up for 24 hours around the June solstice, the midnight Sun, and does not rise at all around the December solstice. The number 66.6 is simply 90 minus the tilt. Between about 23.4 degrees north and 23.4 degrees south, in the tropics, the Sun passes straight overhead at noon on at least one day a year, and temperatures change less through the year. If Earth had no tilt at all, every place would get close to 12 hours of daylight every day of the year, and there would be almost no seasons. Distance does have a small effect. Because sunlight spreads out as it travels, Earth receives about 7 percent more sunlight in early January than in early July. That is real, but it is outweighed by the tilt, which shifts the noon Sun at any mid-northern latitude by about 47 degrees between June and December. You can watch this shift without any equipment. Stand a stick upright in the ground and mark the tip of its shadow at midday once a month. North of the tropics, the noon shadow is shortest around the June solstice and longest around the December solstice. People have kept this kind of record with upright posts called gnomons since ancient times. Now it is your turn to look up. Starting tonight, keep a sky diary: a notebook or phone note with one short entry for each clear night you look. Write the date, the time, where you stood and what you saw. Sketch the Moon’s shape, note which side is lit, and record where it sits: its compass direction and how many fists it is above the horizon. Then look for a planet. The five planets that are easy to see with your eyes alone, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, all stay close to the ecliptic, the line across the sky that the Sun follows through the year, and they usually shine with a steadier light than the twinkling stars. Venus, when it is up, is the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon. With binoculars held steady, Jupiter shows up to four of its moons as tiny dots beside it. A common misconception: It’s summer because Earth is closer to the Sun. In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter, and its distance changes by only about 3 percent over the year. The seasons are also opposite in the two hemispheres, which distance cannot explain. The 23.4-degree tilt of Earth’s axis changes how high the Sun climbs and how long the days last, and that is what makes the seasons.
